characters: Adamu: a thoughtful ten-year-old Ghanaian boy in a neat teal polo shirt and dark blue shorts, holding a plain unlabelled notebook.
Gadzekpo: his ten-year-old Ghanaian female neighbour and friend with braided pigtails and yellow hair beads, wearing a coral top and denim skirt.
Adamu’s mother: a warm Ghanaian woman in a yellow-and-slate patterned kabah and slit.

narrationPlan.voice: A thoughtful boy’s voice for Adamu; a practical girl’s voice for Gadzekpo
narrationPlan.pace: Practical and clear, like a checklist (about 100 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light, ticking tune like a meter (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Prepaid electricity meters and mobile top-up alerts are familiar across Ghanaian towns and villages. The story follows the NaCCA Basic 4 Science standard on conserving electricity (B4.4.2.1.2).
The weekly meter-reading comparison models the curriculum’s household inquiry project (the figures 18 and 13 units are illustrative story examples).
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?

Check the electricity-conservation strategies against NaCCA B4.4.2.1.2.

teacherGuide.overview: When a household’s prepaid electricity units run low early, two children audit wasted power, practise safe conservation habits, and compare weekly meter readings. Based on NaCCA Basic 4 Science.
learningGoals: Identify at least four practical ways to conserve electricity at home and school.
State key electrical safety rules for children.
Compare weekly electricity use from simple recorded numbers.
beforeReading: Ask: which electrical appliances in a home use the most power when left on unnecessarily?
whileReading: Pause on page 5 and ask learners to calculate how many units the family saved.
afterReading: Conduct a supervised classroom walk to spot lights or fans left on in empty rooms.
Design a visual door reminder for switching off lights.
discussion: Why is ironing clothes in one batch more efficient than heating the iron many separate times?
Why must you never touch a switch with wet hands?
reflection: What is one habit you will start at home today to help save electricity?

mathsExtension.task: Adamu’s family used 18 units in week one and 13 units in week two. How many units did they save in week two?
If the family saves 5 units every week for 4 weeks, how many electricity units do they save altogether?

support: Sort appliance picture cards into “In Use” versus “Wasting Power”.
stretch: Compare incandescent bulbs and LED bulbs to explain why LEDs use fewer units for the same brightness.

culturalNotes: Prepaid electricity meters and mobile top-up alerts are familiar across Ghanaian towns and villages. The story follows the NaCCA Basic 4 Science standard on conserving electricity (B4.4.2.1.2).
The weekly meter-reading comparison models the curriculum’s household inquiry project (the figures 18 and 13 units are illustrative story examples).
localiseThis: Adapt examples to your community’s power supply (prepaid ECG/NEDCo meters, postpaid bills, or solar home systems).
Children must never touch sockets, plugs, hot irons, or loose wires; meter reading is done purely visually with an adult.

factCheck.claim: Switching off unused lights and fans, using daylight, batching high-heat tasks like ironing, unplugging idle electronics, and using LED bulbs reduce household electricity consumption.
factCheck.explanation: Heating elements (irons) and continuous motors/lighting draw steady electrical power (wattage over time = kilowatt-hours/units); reducing runtime and wattage directly lowers kWh consumed.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Science Curriculum for Basic 4 (B4.4.2.1.2) & Energy Commission of Ghana Energy Efficiency Guidelines.
